intro: Thredbo is an alpine village in Kosciuszko National Park, in the Snowy Mountains of New South Wales, below Australia's highest peak. On the slopes near it a reader photographed a snow gum sprawling among granite boulders, its bark streaked grey, cream and olive, one of the rare healthy ones, they write, in a High Country where drought and a native beetle are killing many of the snow gums.

trees.how_to_recognise: A snow gum sprawling among big lichen-crusted granite boulders, several smooth trunks twisting out from one base, their bark streaked grey, cream and olive.
trees.access: In Kosciuszko National Park, on the slopes near Thredbo, reached on foot; park entry fees apply to vehicles. Our pin marks the area.
trees.story:
"Snow Gum dieback is affecting a very large number of the trees across the Australian High Country," wrote the reader who sent us this tree from the slopes near Thredbo in Kosciuszko National Park. "Weakened by drought, a native beetle is now attacking the Snow Gums. This beauty is one of the rare healthy specimens we came across."

Snow gums are the trees of the Australian Alps, the eucalypts that hold the treeline, bent and shaped by snow and wind. This one sprawls among lichen-crusted granite boulders, its trunks twisting out from one base and dividing again and again into a tangle of limbs. The bark is what makes snow gums famous, and here it is at its best: smooth, pale grey streaked with cream and olive, shed in ribbons so that each limb looks freshly painted.

We do not know its age or girth. Snow gums often regrow from a buried root base after fire, so the stems can be much younger than the tree itself. If you know this one, tell us here.

Our pin marks the area on the slope. Look for the granite boulders that cradle its base.
